title: Spot a proposition, then negate and re-implicate it
concepts: A proposition is a declarative sentence with exactly one truth value. Commands ("Open the door."), questions, and open sentences such as x + 5 = 7 with x unbound are not propositions. A false statement like 2 + 3 = 7 still is one, because false is a truth value.

Negate a compound statement by pushing ¬ inward with De Morgan's law: ¬(p ∧ q) becomes ¬p ∨ ¬q and ¬(p ∨ q) becomes ¬p ∧ ¬q. The English form of "The summer in Johor is hot and sunny" therefore uses "or", not "and".

An implication p → q is false only in the single case p true and q false. When the hypothesis is false the implication is true whatever the conclusion says, so "If 0.5 is an integer, then 1 + 0.5 = 3" is true.

From p → q there are three relatives: the converse q → p, the inverse ¬p → ¬q, and the contrapositive ¬q → ¬p. Only the contrapositive is equivalent to the original, which is what makes it useful for direct proofs.

Read necessary and sufficient carefully in English: "p is necessary for q" and "q only if p" both place p in the then-part (q → p), while "p is sufficient for q" gives p → q. Rewriting the sentence as if ..., then ... before assigning symbols keeps the direction right.

example.title: Four English sentences, four symbolic readings
example.explanation: Let p be "your car is out of gas" and q be "you cannot drive your car". Each row below shows how a surface pattern in English maps onto connectives, and the check is always to identify the hypothesis first, then the conclusion.
steps: "Your car is not out of gas" is simply ¬p.
"You cannot drive your car if it is out of gas" puts the if-part first in meaning: p → q.
"Your car is not out of gas if you can drive it" has hypothesis "you can drive it" (¬q) and conclusion ¬p, so ¬q → ¬p, the contrapositive of p → q and therefore equivalent to it.
"If you cannot drive your car then it is out of gas" is q → p, the converse, which is not equivalent to the original claim.

title: Read a truth table as a CNF or a DNF
concepts: A conjunctive normal form is a conjunction of disjunctions of variables or their negations, for example (p ∨ q) ∧ (p ∨ ¬q) ∧ (¬p ∨ ¬q). A disjunctive normal form reverses the nesting: disjunctions of conjunctions, such as (p ∧ ¬q ∧ ¬r) ∨ (¬p ∧ ¬q ∧ r).
Every compound proposition is equivalent to a CNF and to a DNF, so the two forms are alternative readings of the same truth table rather than different functions.
A normal form is full when no variable is missing from any bracket. Fullness matters because only then does each bracket describe exactly one row of the truth table.

Build the full CNF from the rows where the result is false: one clause per such row, in which a variable appears negated when the row values it true and un-negated when the row values it false. The clause must be false for that row alone.
Build the full DNF from the rows where the result is true: one term per such row, with each variable written exactly as that row values it. If a row is true for p = T and q = F the term is (p ∧ ¬q).

example.title: Both normal forms of [(p ↔ q) ⊕ ¬p] → ¬q
example.explanation: The tutorial works this proposition out for two variables, so the truth table has four rows. Its result column is false for (p, q) = (T, T) and for (F, T), and true for (T, F) and (F, F). Each row then supplies exactly one bracket, and the two answers must describe the same column.
steps: False row (T, T): both variables are true, so both enter negated and joined by ∨, giving (¬p ∨ ¬q).
False row (F, T): p is false so it enters plain, q is true so it enters negated, giving (p ∨ ¬q). Conjoin the two clauses: full CNF is (¬p ∨ ¬q) ∧ (p ∨ ¬q).
True row (T, F): read the values as they stand, giving (p ∧ ¬q). True row (F, F) gives (¬p ∧ ¬q). Disjoin them: full DNF is (p ∧ ¬q) ∨ (¬p ∧ ¬q).
Check either form against one row, for example (F, T): CNF gives (T ∨ F) ∧ (F ∨ F) = F, matching the table. The shared factor ¬q in both answers is the signal that the same column was read twice.

title: Translate between English and nested quantifiers
concepts: A predicate such as L(x, y) is "x likes y": it becomes a proposition only once every variable is bound by a quantifier and the universe of discourse is fixed. Naming the universe is part of the answer, because the same formula can be true over people and false over integers.

The universal quantifier ∀x P(x) pairs with → and the existential pairs with ∧. "Every parrot is ugly" is ∀x (P(x) → U(x)); writing it with ∧ instead claims that everything in the universe is an ugly parrot.

Order matters in nested quantifiers. ∀x ∃y L(x, y) says everyone likes someone, and the person liked may differ from one x to the next, while ∃y ∀x L(x, y) says one single person is liked by everybody. The second implies the first, never the reverse.
Negation rules for quantifiers mirror De Morgan: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x) and ¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x). In English, "not every student has a book" means "some student has no book".

Work a translation in four steps: fix the universe, define the predicates, choose the quantifier for each noun phrase, then apply the connective rule (∀ with →, ∃ with ∧). Claims such as "no books are expensive" are universal conditionals with a negated conclusion, ∀x (B(x) → ¬E(x)).

example.title: "Some student does not have any book"
example.explanation: Take S(x) for "x is a student", B(y) for "y is a book" and H(x, y) for "x has y", with the universe of discourse being all objects. The sentence contains one existential claim about a student and one negated existential claim about books, so two quantifiers are needed.
steps: Universe and predicates are already declared, so nothing needs to be restricted to people or to books by hand.
"Some student" is ∃x S(x) and the two parts must be joined with ∧, because the object asserted to exist has to be a student.
"does not have any book" denies the existence of a book that x has: ¬∃y (B(y) ∧ H(x, y)), equivalently ∀y (B(y) → ¬H(x, y)).
Put them together: ∃x (S(x) ∧ ∀y (B(y) → ¬H(x, y))). Compare it with ∃x (S(x) ∧ ∀y (B(y) ∧ H(x, y))), which is the different claim that some student has every book.

title: Run the three steps of an induction proof
concepts: Mathematical induction proves a statement P(n) for every integer from a chosen start upwards. The domino picture names the two obligations: something must tip the first domino, and each domino must tip the next one.

Step 1, the basis step, verifies P for the first value. For sums written 1 + 2 + ... + n that is usually n = 1, but a statement about non-negative integers starts at n = 0, where 1 + 2 + ... + 2^n reduces to the single term 2^0 = 1.

Step 2, the inductive hypothesis, states P(k) and assumes it. Step 3, the inductive step, uses that assumption to prove P(k + 1). Writing both sides of P(k + 1) before substituting the hypothesis shows how much work the assumption actually does.

Divisibility proofs follow the same pattern with algebra: rewrite the (k + 1) expression so that it contains a multiple of the k expression plus a leftover that is visibly divisible. To move from 7^k − 2^k to 7^(k+1) − 2^(k+1), multiply the hypothesis by 7 and add back 5·2^k.

Close with the conclusion the method licenses: because the basis holds and P(k) → P(k + 1) holds, P(n) is true for all n from the starting value onwards. A missing basis step leaves the chain unstarted, no matter how clean the inductive step is.

example.title: Prove 1 + 2 + 2^2 + ... + 2^n = 2^(n+1) − 1 for n ≥ 0
example.explanation: The statement is about non-negative integers, so the chain begins at 0 rather than 1. The inductive step is a two-line algebraic argument: split the sum at the last term, then use the hypothesis on the part that remains.
steps: Basis step: P(0) says 2^0 = 2^1 − 1, i.e. 1 = 1, which is true.

Inductive step: 1 + 2 + ... + 2^k + 2^(k+1) = (2^(k+1) − 1) + 2^(k+1) by the hypothesis, and the two powers of 2 combine to 2·2^(k+1) = 2^(k+2), giving 2^(k+2) − 1 = 2^((k+1)+1) − 1, which is exactly P(k + 1).
Conclusion: by mathematical induction the formula holds for every non-negative integer n. Notice that the basis step used n = 0; starting the sum at 1 would have left P(0) unproved.
